title: Promoting Resilience After High-Risk Birth: 2see2act2gether
summary:
Background:
Premature infants and other high-risk newborns may experience long-term health and developmental consequences. Problems with neurological development as well as heart and lung function are particularly common.
Due to their immaturity, these children are also more sensitive to stress and strain surrounding birth and during treatment in the neonatal unit. Such experiences can influence their future development. Long-term developmental trajectories vary from child to child. Resilience—that is, a child’s ability to cope with stress and difficult situations while still developing well—may play an important role here. This study aims to examine the development and resilience of preschool-aged children who were born prematurely or at high risk.

Research Questions:
- How do preterm infants develop in the long term, particularly with regard to cardiac, pulmonary, and neurological development?
- Which parameters can help us better understand and predict different long-term developmental trajectories?
- Can everyday support offers—in this case, through a music education intervention—improve development and, in particular, the ability to cope with stress and external influences?

Methodology:
The study examines the physical, neurological, and psychomotor development of preschool-aged children who were born prematurely or at high risk, as well as the influence of stressors before and after birth and the social environment.
The study compares various groups, such as: preterm and full-term infants, children with varying degrees of maturity at birth, children with varying levels of health-related stress during the preschool years, and children at different levels of development (delayed vs. age-typical).
In addition, the study examines how stress markers change before and after a music intervention, as well as how stress markers and the children’s development change over the entire intervention period.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Study cohort I: Preschool-aged children born prematurely
This cohort includes premature infants with a gestational age of 23+0 to 36+6
completed weeks of gestation who were cared for at the Perinatal Center of the Universitätsklinik für Kinder- und Jugendmedizin Oldenburg and have reached preschool age.

Study Cohort II: Term Newborns Classified by Birth Risk at
Preschool Age
In order to interpret the results obtained from the preterm infants over the course of the longitudinal study, term newborns classified by birth risk with a gestational age at birth of 37+0 to 41 weeks, as well as their parents or legal guardians, are being recruited.
Exclusion criteria:
• Lack of communication channels to inform the parents
• Severe congenital anomalies diagnosed prenatally or postnatally with
cardiopulmonary dysfunction that are incompatible with medium-term survival
(severe pulmonary hypoplasia with anhydramnios, hypoplastic left ventricle,
Ebstein’s anomaly, total anomalous pulmonary venous connection)
• Presence of a diaphragmatic hernia or confirmed trisomy 13 or 18
• Metabolic disorders that result in impairment of the entire organism
